newsitem.title: USA: IMF chief predicts success for European currency.
newsitem.headline: IMF chief predicts success for European currency.

text.p: IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus pronounced himself satisfied with the health of the world economy on Thursday and predicted Europe would succeed in its tough task of launching a single currency in 1999.
"We are working in a kind of satisfactory global environment," the International Monetary Fund chief told reporters ahead of the start of the IMF/World Bank semi-annual meeting here later this week.
The IMF on Wednesday forecast that world economic growth will pick up to 4.1 percent next year, from 3.8 percent in 1996, but singled out Europe as one possible source of concern.

Camdessus said he sees better times ahead for Europe and voiced confidence that many European countries will be able to meet the tough budget criteria set out for participation in the new European Monetary System in 1999.
"I am confident that on Friday, Jan. 1, 1999 you will have the new Euro system started," Camdessus proclaimed.

Speaking to reporters at a separate briefing, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin also called the global economic outlook "encouraging," although he expressed some reservations about prospects for Europe and Japan.
"Prospects have improved in Japan and Europe, but growth in those regions still looks quite moderate," Rubin said.
He said it was "critically important" that Japan continue to pursue policies aimed at promoting domestic demand-led growth. "We are of course always interested in growth in Europe, too," he added.

On Saturday, Rubin will meet finance ministers and central bankers from the rest of the Group of Seven -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and Japan. That gathering will take place on the fringes of the IMF/World Bank meeting.
The G7 is expected to discuss currency market movements as well as the health of the world economy when it meets on Saturday.
The dollar has been buoyant recently, but Rubin evinced little sign of concern that would undercut the competitiveness of U.S. exports on world markets.
He called the U.S. economy "very healthy," declared American industry competitive and repeated his backing for a strong dollar.
The IMF's Camdessus also saw little reason for concern about recent currency movements.
"The key currencies are now in ... a solid, well-justified constellation and we don't forsee major changes in the near future," Camdessus told Reuters Financial Television.

The IMF official also gave reporters some insight into a controversial plan for the lending agency to sell off a small amount of its gold to help finance a new programme to help the very poorest debt-laden countries as well as to make an existing programme permanent.

He said the hierarchy of the international community had committed itself to both goals, making clear that the issue of gold sales that had divided some of the largest member countries would only need to be addressed if funds from other sources were insufficient.
"This is a done deal," Camdessus told reporters.

He also made clear that the IMF's own finances were beginning to run short and that the lending agency needed to get approval for "a substantial" increase in its quotas, or underlying economic base, sometime in the period ahead so that it would enter the new century in good economic shape.
Camdessus in the past has said that the IMF would need a doubling of its economic base to around $400 billion, but he defined what he called a substantial increase in the quotas as 50 to 100 percent.
The IMF has been hard hit by the need to make vast loans to Russia and Mexico last year.
